extracted.intended_audience: general public, researchers, policymakers, and practitioners interested in misinformation and countermeasures
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes strategies, mechanisms, and considerations for detecting, countering, and preventing misinformation online (crowdsourcing, one-on-one/social correction, prebunking, platform and policy interventions, and limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourcing effectiveness — Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The user must trust the source of the fact-check (i.e., the crowd).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust is necessary for crowdsourced corrections to be accepted; however, in-group crowds are trusted but may not provide dissonance, while out-group crowds may be dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourcing effectiveness — Cognitive Dissonance
rubrics_metrics.description: The correction must be sufficiently different from the user's prior beliefs to create dissonance and encourage a belief update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective corrections should produce enough cognitive conflict to motivate reconsideration, but if too far outside a person's worldview they may be rejected as from a hostile out-group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourcing effectiveness — Crowd Size and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficiently large and diverse crowd is needed for accuracy and to establish a social norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bigger, diverse crowds improve factual accuracy and help normalize corrected information; small or homogeneous crowds risk bias and reduced credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-steps-away network approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect users with fact-checking crowds from communities just outside their immediate ideological echo chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a perspective that is novel enough to create dissonance but not so distant as to be dismissed as a hostile out-group; recommended to resolve trust vs. dissonance trade-offs in crowdsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-on-one correction strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal interactions can be effective when they leverage social ties and communication style rather than just presenting facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivering facts alone is often ineffective. Belief change is more likely when information comes from close social ties (friends/family). Strategies include instilling doubt and encouraging examination of belief roots; use empathetic tone to keep channels open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social correction — three recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: When correcting misinformation publicly on social media (social correction), use evidence, repetition, and alternatives to increase efficacy for observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers recommend: (1) include a link to a credible source of relevant information (e.g., expert organization); (2) repeat the correct information (for example at the beginning and end of a comment); (3) offer an alternative explanation. Note: tone may affect how the target receives the message (and engagement) but is less likely to change how observers perceive accuracy. Be aware social correction can sometimes amplify the original post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prebunking / inoculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventive strategy that 'inoculates' people by showing examples of misinformation and how it works before exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prebunking focuses on identifying common logical fallacies and deceptive tactics (e.g., emotional appeals, false dichotomies, ad hominem) and common misinformation sources. Research shows promising results; education-based inoculations (including videos) are being explored for adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated detection systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use automated systems to flag or add context and resources to content suspected of misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-level automated detection can surface questionable content and attach corrective context or links; must be designed to respect privacy and minimize errors and overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance-enhancing technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies that better enable people to determine the veracity and origins of a claim, image, or video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provenance tools (metadata, provenance standards) can help users and platforms assess authenticity and source reliability; useful for combating manipulated media and deepfakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: APIs for research
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide APIs and data access for researchers to detect, understand, and counter misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-provided APIs enable independent analysis and development of countermeasures; access policies must balance research needs and privacy/security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active bystanders / corrective commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage bystander interventions (users leaving corrective comments) to counter misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active bystanders can spread corrections socially; training or nudges to encourage constructive corrective commenting may enhance reach of accurate information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use unpaid/volunteer community moderation to identify and manage misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community moderators can scale platform oversight, but volunteers are often untrained and independent—systems should support fairness, consistency, and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-virals (message-forwarding limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the number of times a message can be forwarded in privacy-respecting encrypted chats to slow spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical constraints on virality (forward limits, throttling) can reduce rapid amplification in private messaging while preserving privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective intelligence (platforms like Wikipedia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage systems where multiple editors/refiners and peer evaluation improve content accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models like Wikipedia or Q&A sites with community evaluation harness collective scrutiny; combine with transparency and citation standards for reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthy institutions and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen and promote institutions and datasets that users can rely on as authoritative sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighting and linking to trustworthy institutions and verified data sources increases correction credibility and helps observers assess truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media literacy education
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase citizens' ability to use ICTs to find, evaluate, create, and communicate information (teaching media/information literacy across ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal education (e.g., K–12 mandates, curricula) and adult-focused inoculation/education programs improve long-term resilience; examples include Estonia's nationwide program and New Jersey's K–12 mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid heavy-handed removal; build resilience and healthy information environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend building resilience and a healthy online information environment rather than broadly removing offending content; caution that censorship can push communities to harder-to-address corners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should weigh trade-offs: removals may reduce visibility but risk driving groups to fringe platforms; prioritize resilience, transparency, and measured interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-based interventions (pre-, during-, post-exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt interventions tailored to stages of misinformation spread: prior to exposure (education/inoculation), during spread (detection, ranking), and after exposure (corrections and collaborator messaging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective programs combine pre-exposure education, technological detection/ranking and bot identification, and post-exposure corrective messaging; topic-specific mixes (e.g., climate change) may include fines or other consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intermediaries credible to target audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus corrective efforts on intermediaries (activists, politicians, community leaders) who are trusted by those holding false beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediaries sharing corrections can overcome identity-based resistance; select messengers who share identities/worldviews with the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize association of misinformation with political/group identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid framing corrections in ways that reinforce political or group identity ties to the misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide corrections from nonpartisan experts and avoid false balance; decouple factual corrections from partisan identity to increase acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize corrections that are hard to avoid or deny
rubrics_metrics.description: Use corrections grounded in observable, hard-to-dispute facts (e.g., economic indicators, documented extreme weather events) to reduce denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual, verifiable examples that are salient and difficult to reframe increase lasting correction efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI tools for fact-checking and media forensics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply AI to fact-check claims in real time and to detect fabricated audio/video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms can flag likely false claims and detect deepfakes; these tools are being developed but require validation, transparency, and safeguards against misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI for information and media literacy education
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AI to support education initiatives in information and media literacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI-driven tutors, examples, and interactive prebunking tools can scale literacy training; design for accessibility and empirically demonstrated efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote peer review and vetting for online content
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage systems that require or simulate vetting, review, or citation practices to improve accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because online content bypasses traditional editorial/peer review, promoting verification, source attribution, expert review, or community vetting can raise overall quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for persistence of misinformation and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interventions that recognize misinformation can persist after corrections and that corrections must reach the right audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider long-term follow-ups, repeated corrections, targeted dissemination beyond science-focused channels, and strategies for preventing re-exposure-induced relapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backfire effect assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: While backfire effects (corrections strengthening false beliefs) were proposed, evidence suggests they are rare or limited; interventions should be aware but not assume them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should monitor for potential subgroup backfire but rely on evidence that for most people corrections do not have negative effects; avoid overgeneralizing early backfire findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor unintended effects on belief discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware interventions might reduce belief in both false and true information, potentially undermining the ability to discriminate veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies found inoculation/accuracy primes can reduce discrimination between plausible and implausible conspiracy theories; evaluate ecosystem-level trade-offs and base-rate effects.
